_README: Pre-existing violations this gate INHERITED, not ones it tolerates. Each row is a known
dangling published command that predates the gate and is owned by another lane.
The baseline is SELF-RETIRING and that is what stops it becoming slack: if a row stops
violating, the gate FAILS and tells you to delete the row. A baseline that can only grow
is a mute button; one that fails when it is stale is a ratchet. Adding a row is a
deliberate act with an owner and a settling action recorded next to it.
This file may not be used to silence a NEW violation. The correct fixes, in order:
1. `git add` the target -- it is evidence someone is expected to rerun.
2. stop publishing it as a runnable command.
3. only then, and only for another lane's tree, a row here.
_RETIRED: Both inherited rows named `platform/lib/_p12_refute_predicate.py`, and both are GONE
because the violation is gone: the file is now tracked (SLOP build round 3, 26155108).
The blocker those rows recorded was real -- one `F841` at line 107 would have turned
`gate-lint-format` red repo-wide -- and their settling_action proposed deleting the unused
binding. That was not done: it would edit another lane's evidence bytes, which is exactly
what both earlier SLOP rounds declined and were vindicated for. Instead `ruff.toml` gained
which silences that one rule on that one path, keeps the file inside `ruff format --check`
(an `extend-exclude` entry would not), and leaves every other rule live on it. Controlled
both ways: the same F841 shape at a different path is still flagged rc 1, and `ruff check`
over the 14 cited files went rc 1 -> rc 0.
The floor is now ZERO inherited violations. The next row added here has no predecessor to

entries.owner: the platform / generated-SSOT lane, not SLOP
why: Surfaced the moment `platform/` entered this gate's corpus (SLOP build round 3).
Unlike the other nine rows the widening exposed, this target DOES NOT EXIST on disk --
`platform/lib/ssot/` has no `verify.py`. So it is not bucket (b) evidence that merely
went uncommitted; it is a published command naming a file nobody has. The other nine
were all real files on one disk and were committed in the same change.
Carried as a row rather than fixed because the correct fix is a judgement this lane
cannot make: either the script was never written, or it was renamed, and only the
settling_action: The owning lane either commits the script at that path, or edits
`platform/architecture/generated-ssot.md` to stop publishing it as a runnable command
(a `<!-- published-command-example: platform/lib/ssot/verify.py -->` marker on the line
is the supported way to say `illustrative, not runnable`), then deletes this row.
The gate FAILS while the row is stale, so it cannot rot.
